milestone.title: Macintosh reaches the public
milestone.note: Steve Jobs’s January 30 Boston Computer Society presentation put the mouse-driven graphical computer before the world’s largest personal-computer user organization.

editorNote: Six days after its unveiling, Macintosh meets an experienced public audience; elsewhere, IBM draws a hard legal line around the code inside PC compatibility.
morningLine: The mouse takes the stage in Boston while the clone business heads for court.

lead.headline: Macintosh Meets the Public in Boston
lead.dek: Steve Jobs brings Apple’s new graphical computer before the Boston Computer Society for its first public demonstration.
body: BOSTON, Jan. 30 — Six days after Apple formally introduced Macintosh, Steve Jobs carried the compact computer onto the Boston Computer Society stage for what the society’s founder remembers as its first public showing. Before a room of experienced personal-computer users, the machine’s windows, icons and mouse moved from advertising promise to a working demonstration.

Jobs showed point-and-click commands, cutting and pasting between applications, mixed text and pictures, drawing tools, stacked desktop documents and even three-dimensional chess. The sequence made Apple’s central argument visible: ordinary work could be directed through consistent pictures and menus instead of a memorized command language.

The $2,495 launch model combines 128 kilobytes of RAM, 64 kilobytes of ROM, a built-in high-resolution monochrome display, a mouse and a 3.5-inch disk drive. Apple is including MacWrite and MacPaint for purchasers during the first 100 days, giving buyers immediate demonstrations of proportional type, page composition and bitmap drawing.

Microsoft Multiplan is available at launch, while Apple says more than 100 outside companies are developing products. The company also says its Fremont line can turn out one Macintosh every 27 seconds, but expects demand to outrun supply for several months.

The Boston appearance supplies the crucial test missing from launch-day spectacle: how the system behaves in front of knowledgeable users. Macintosh is still a costly, memory-tight first model, but its public debut makes the graphical desktop a concrete personal-computing proposition.

stories.headline: IBM Takes the Clone War to Court
body: IBM has sued makers of PC-compatible products over copyrighted code, putting the industry on notice that an open hardware bus does not make the PC’s basic input-output system free to copy. The ROM software at issue is what lets compatible hardware behave like an IBM machine.

The pressure separates functional compatibility from literal duplication. Vendors that want to share the IBM PC software market will need independently written BIOS code—a legal and engineering path that promises to shape which clone makers survive.

stories.headline: Lisa 2 Becomes Macintosh’s Elder Sibling
body: Apple has introduced three Lisa 2 models alongside Macintosh, describing the systems as one 32-bit graphical family. The revised Lisa line adopts the smaller 3.5-inch disk format and is intended to share software with the less expensive Macintosh.

The pairing gives Apple a ladder from the $2,495 compact desktop to higher-end office machines. February’s BYTE puts Macintosh on its cover while also examining Lisa 2, capturing Apple’s attempt to turn a new interface into a product family.

stories.headline: MacWrite and MacPaint Make the Desktop Tangible
body: MacWrite handles multiple fonts and sizes, search and replace, and pictures pasted into documents. MacPaint supplies brushes, pencils, erasers, textures and geometric shapes for bitmap illustration.

Bundling both programs during the first 100 days is more than a promotion: the pair demonstrates shared menus, cut and paste, proportional type and mixed graphics immediately after the box is opened. Microsoft Multiplan adds a familiar business application to the launch shelf.

stories.headline: Computer Games Ask What Comes After the Crash
body: February’s COMPUTE! asks both “What Makes A Good Game?” and “The Future Of Electronic Games” as the American cartridge-console trade contracts. The magazine’s machine-spanning coverage suggests that inventive play is migrating toward programmable home computers.

Its review of Computer War for Atari, VIC-20 and TI machines places nuclear strategy in the post-WarGames wave. The evidence is a monthly trend rather than a precise release diary, but it shows designers and players looking beyond arcade imitation toward deeper simulations.
